extracted.intended_audience: scholars, journal editors, grant reviewers, and policymakers concerned with peer review and research evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how reviewers convert multiple, heterogeneous peer-review criteria into a single measure of merit (commensuration), how that process creates systematic biases in manuscript and grant decisions, and what structural reforms might reduce those biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensuration (conversion of heterogeneous criteria into a single metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must convert a submission’s strengths and weaknesses on heterogeneous peer review criteria into a single metric of quality or merit (the process of commensuration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper identifies this conversion process itself as important for understanding review outcomes: how reviewers aggregate and weight distinct criterion-level judgments when producing an overall evaluation is a central locus for bias. Attention should be paid to the methods and heuristics reviewers use to translate multiple criterion judgments into one score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensuration bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A new kind of peer review bias that arises when the process of commensuration systematically privileges some criteria over others, producing distorted publication and funding patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commensuration bias explains how systematic prioritization of certain criteria permits problematic patterns (e.g., under-rewarding replication, risk-taking, or methodological rigor). Identification of commensuration bias requires examining which criteria are systematically upweighted or downweighted during aggregation and whether that produces inequitable or epistemically harmful outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic prioritization / weighting of peer review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency for reviewers and review systems to prioritize some peer review criteria (e.g., novelty, perceived prestige, statistically significant/positive results) over others (e.g., replication value, methodological rigor, risky/transformative ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate review behavior and institutional incentives to see which criteria receive more weight in practice. The article links such prioritization to problematic publication/funding patterns and cites literature on publication bias, conservatism in peer review, and incentives to favor hypothesis-testing and positive results. Detecting this requires looking beyond formal criteria to actual decision behavior and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of overall impact/summary score versus separate criterion scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrast between producing a single overall evaluation (overall impact/quality) and reporting separate criterion-level scores for different dimensions of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights the step where reviewers collapse criterion-level judgments into an overall score as a site of bias; using and analyzing separate criterion scores can reveal differential weighting and may help diagnose sources of disparity (for example, references note that criterion scores can account for racial disparities in overall impact scores). Consider policies that preserve and make transparent criterion-level information to reduce opaque aggregation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring publication and funding outcome patterns as evidence of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing downstream patterns — e.g., prevalence of positive results, rates of replication publication, distribution of awards across topics, institutions, and demographics — as indicators of commensuration-related distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that commensuration bias permits and facilitates problematic patterns of publication and funding; practical evaluation should therefore include empirical outcome measures (publication rates of negative/replication studies, award distributions, discipline- or demographic-based disparities) to detect and quantify the effect of commensuration on the research ecosystem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural strategies to realign peer review practices with the aims of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional and procedural reforms intended to reduce commensuration bias and better align review processes and incentives with epistemic goals (the article 'foregrounds a range of structural strategies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the abstract does not enumerate specific reforms in full, the paper points to institutional-level changes (e.g., altering scoring procedures, changing incentive structures, increasing transparency of criterion weighting, adopting alternative decision mechanisms) as routes to mitigate commensuration bias. Policies to consider include preserving criterion-level scores, redesigning reviewer guidance to discourage implicit over-weighting of certain criteria, and structural changes at journals and funding agencies to reward replication, rigor, and risk-taking.
